newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Big calendar spread in BT.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Big calendar spread in BT.

text.p: A huge calendar spread took place in British Telecom call options, prompting traders to wonder if it could be linked to a planned merger between BT and MCI Communications Corp.

BT's October 60 calls and January 60 calls traded 6,060 contracts each in a deal recorded as a spread on the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) at premiums of 9 and 9-7/8 respectively, or net exchange of 7/8.
The brokerage which brought in the order was also said to have crossed 600,000 shares of the underlying BT American Depositary Receipts on the New York Stock Exchange at 69-1/4.

Jon Najarian, president of Mercury Trading at CBOE, said an end-user appeared to have sold the October and bought the January to roll out his exposure by three months, perhaps in anticipation that the $20 billion merger would take more time before it could be finalized.
"Usually a customer rolls an option from one month to another when they think that their timeframe has changed but they want to stay with their investment," he said.
"It could be that that the customer thought that the deal between MCI and British Telecom might not close until after the October expiration," he added.
Traders said MCI's profit warning last month had cast some shadows over the merger deal.
But Najarian noted that the true intention of the deal was unclear and that it could be linked to dividends or the customer's position in MCI stocks.

Indeed, one options trader said the deal could well have been a simple dividend play as the BT stock was due to go ex-dividend next week on August 13 and premium for October 60 calls had contained virtually no time value that would be wasted by exercising.

In a typical dividend play, a trader buys deep in-the-money calls and sells similar calls as a hedge, exercising the long position before the ex-dividend day to collect the payout and hoping the shorts would not be exercised.

Michael Schwartz, a managing director of Oppenheimer & Co, suggested that the deal might have consisted of two parts -- covered call writing by the end-user in the January calls, and the brokerage buying -- and probably exercising -- the October calls to facilitate the cross in the stock.

"If the customer was the buyer (of the stock against short January call position), they (brokerage) excercised the Oct 60s and used that stock to sell to the customer that they crossed it with," Schwartz said.

"The way the Oct 60s traded at parity, I've got to believe they exercised them," he added, noting that neither the October 60s nor the January 60s had any significant open interest that would have laid ground for a roll-over.
